summary: Describes using the ACAP protocol to configure wireless devices over the air, covering activation and provisioning of phones. It is an informational paper and replaced RFC 2604.

eli5.summary: Instead of visiting a shop to set up a phone, the phone gets its settings by a message through the air. This paper explains one way to do that.

questions: how does acap provision a phone
subtitle: How a carrier could provision and update CDMA phones over the air using ACAP, a small Internet configuration protocol.

tldr.problem: Carriers want to activate handsets and update their settings over the air instead of in shops, but the standard IS-683A equipment for this is costly.
tldr.mechanism: The phone makes an IS-707 data call, opens a TCP connection to a provisioning server running ACAP, authenticates, and downloads only the settings that changed.
tldr.outcome: This informational paper argues ACAP is a cheap, open and extensible fit for the job, and compares it with IS-683A over TCP/IP and browser-based forms.

today: RFC 2636 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2604, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. It is a 1999 proposal, not a standard, and the text does not say whether any carrier adopted it.

sections.title: Why Provision Phones Over the Air
sections.content:
Wireless carriers want cheaper ways to sell handsets through retail and to activate users and update handset parameters. This memo describes OTASP (Over-the-air Service Provisioning), which lets a new subscriber activate service or an existing one change it without a third party, and OTAPA (Over-the-air Parameter Administration), which lets the carrier update a phone's stored parameters remotely.

The standard way, IS-683A, needs dedicated equipment whose cost pushed carriers to look for alternatives. The memo instead leans on IS-707 data services that carriers were already rolling out, and uses the Internet's ACAP protocol to carry the provisioning data.

OTAPA is pitched as especially useful for mass changes that affect every handset, such as area-code splits.
sections.eli5: Setting up a phone at a shop takes time and money. This paper shows a way for the phone to set itself up through the air.

sections.title: How Activation and Updates Work
sections.content:
For initial provisioning, the subscriber first gives the provider credit information and the phone's ESN. The memo lists three ways: a voice call to a customer care representative, a forms scenario in a browser on the phone, or a desktop scenario using a web browser or in-store kiosk.

Once the user is authorized, a record is created in the network's HLR and a limited-time password tied to the ESN is created. In the voice case the user then dials a special number of the form *228 XX <N-digit password> SEND, which makes the phone start a provisioning session. The carrier chooses N as a trade-off between security and user inconvenience.

Already-authorized users can run OTASP again, for example when the carrier upgrades parameters or needs to troubleshoot. OTAPA is started from the customer care center, either by queuing a notification (one-way SMS or special caller-ID) or by putting a recheck interval in the provisioning data so phones check in periodically. OTAPA can be ended at any time by user call activity.
sections.eli5: The shop gives you a secret code that works for a short time. You type it into the phone, and the phone then fetches its own settings.

sections.title: What Phones and Servers Must Support
sections.content:
Data-based OTASP/OTAPA needs a carrier network with IS-707 data services, either Packet Data Service (IS-707.5) or Quick-Net-Connect. The mobile station must support IS-707 data, RLP, PPP, IP, a transport such as TCP, authentication (optionally encryption), application software for the provisioning protocol, and enough DNS to find the server, unless the address arrives during PPP negotiation.

The provisioning server replaces the IS-683A OTAF. It sits on an IP network inside the carrier, must do everything the OTAF does, and must have an interface to the carrier's Mobile Terminal Authorizing System so its data stays in sync. It must be able to authenticate both the phone and itself. A standard ACAP server is described as an excellent way to meet these needs.

On security, OTASP requires the phone to be validated to the server, while OTAPA requires the phone to validate the server. The server must either generate A-keys with Diffie-Hellman or receive them from the carrier network. End-to-end encryption is listed as a future enhancement.
sections.eli5: The phone needs to be able to make a data call and talk over the Internet. The company needs one server that holds every phone's settings.

sections.title: ACAP as the Provisioning Protocol
sections.content:
ACAP stores configuration data in datasets made of entries, which hold attributes and values, and datasets are hierarchical. Servers support inheritance: items physically in one dataset logically appear in datasets that inherit from it. The memo uses this so a preferred roaming list can live in a regional group dataset and appear automatically in every phone's record in that region, with no work by the phone.

Provisioning data lives in an OTAP dataset class. Each phone has records under /OTAP/USER/<esn>/<nam>/, which allows several NAMs per ESN. Items named Provision.* are downloaded to the phone; items named Client.* are what the phone stores back. Values use the same formats as IS-683A, so IS-683A handset code can be reused.

The phone is a small state machine. After authenticating it searches the Provision.Requested-Data entry to learn what the server wants to know (for example make, model, software revision and free NVRAM), stores those values in its Client entry, then searches for provisioning items whose modtime is newer than the last one it saw. After saving them to NVRAM it stores the new modtime as an acknowledgement, logs out and ends the call.

An administrative client uses the same ACAP commands to load and update records, set inheritance, and report on phones that have not yet been updated.
sections.eli5: The server keeps a folder for every phone, and some settings are shared from a bigger folder. The phone only asks for what changed since its last visit.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
The phone authenticates to the ACAP server before doing anything else, using its ESN and a shared secret. A provisioned phone derives the secret from its A-key; an unprovisioned phone uses the limited-time password. ACAP's baseline mechanism is CRAM-MD5: the secret plus a random challenge from the server goes through a keyed MD5 hash, which the memo likens to the random challenge and CAVE algorithm in IS-683A. A-keys are generated by a Diffie-Hellman exchange, as in IS-683A.

Because ACAP uses SASL, stronger mechanisms can be added later without breaking deployed clients, and IPSec could also be rolled out. The memo prefers basic ACAP authentication for first implementations because it is simple and all procedures are in place.

The Security Considerations section is brief. It says that security is discussed throughout and covers unauthorized updating of handsets, usurpation of newly created accounts, compromise of handset security values, and disclosure of carrier proprietary data and handset parameters.
sections.eli5: The phone and server prove who they are with a secret handshake, so a stranger cannot reprogram your phone.

sections.title: Alternatives and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo weighs ACAP against two options. IS-683A over TCP/IP would mirror the existing protocol closely, so the phone shares software and most procedures are defined. Its drawbacks are that the OTAF server must be custom built, it has no data management features, it needs a proprietary interface, and it still needs end-to-end encryption.

Browser-based forms would put provisioning data in custom tags on web pages. That needs a new meta-protocol and specification, custom software at both ends, a provisioning-capable browser in every phone, and heavy carrier customization.

The memo also separates network-resident data (account status, billing) from configuration data that must persist in the handset. It suggests the web for the first and ACAP for the second. ACAP can coexist with WAP-based provisioning, as long as the WAP server contains a small ACAP client or an interface to an ACAP server. It also notes that OTASP over data is data-only for now, unlike IS-683A, which is inherently simultaneous voice and data.
sections.eli5: The author compares three ways to send settings to phones and explains why the small, simple one looks best to the author.
